transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-10-09 15:00 UTC | Duration 55 minutes | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Oscar (Redwood SE), Lina (Redwood SE), Evan, Priya, Samir, Anna (Triton).

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. quick agenda: we want to go over last week's bench pulses, look at where the tail latency popped, and agree next steps.
[00:22] Evan: yeah, thanks. we ran your script against our staging cluster over the weekend - saw overall tokens per second improvements but at times the p95 jumped, especially during cold starts.
[00:38] Oscar: right, that's consistent with what we saw. the median's down about 18% from the incumbent but the tail is spikier for queries that hit new KV cache pages.
[01:05] Priya: can you remind me which model variant you were using for the runs? i think you mentioned a quantized 4-bit variant?
[01:15] Oscar: yes, we used q4xh variant for the throughput runs and a full fp16 for the low-latency single-shot tests. i think there was an oversubscription on batch sizing in the burst profile.
[01:38] Samir: quick note — our k8s nodes are mixed C5n and G5 in staging, autoscaler set to conservative. baseline vendor used larger static nodes so their cold-warm behavior differs.
[01:55] Speaker 1: mmm hmm, mm-hmm.
[02:08] Lina: i'll share the exact run commands in the deck link in the chat after. a couple of things to call out: our routing policy hit a fallback path during one run which forced a model swap to a compatible variant and that added about 120ms on the p99 for those minutes.
[02:28] Anna: wait, fallback? i thought we'd pinned the model version for the test.
[02:35] Oscar: you did pin it but the runtime triggered a fallback because a GPU on instance-7 OOM'd and our automated policy switched to a smaller variant to maintain throughput. that's why the tail looks worse for a short window.
[02:52] Evan: ah, that would explain the spike around 02:12 in the CSV.
[03:05] Maya: quick pause — let's annotate that in the sheet as a fallback event. we'll mark any run with model-swaps as outlier unless you want us to keep them.
[03:18] Evan: mark as outlier please, we want fair apples-to-apples comparing steady state.
[03:24] Oscar: agreed. for steady-state throughput, our batching and prefix caching saved about 22% CPU cycles per token. however, the cold-start sequences (first token after idle) are slower due to KV deserialization cost.
[03:46] Priya: are you using radix cache or your prefix-only cache? because our baseline had a larger on-disk LM cache layer.
[03:55] Lina: it's the prefix+kv hybrid. sometimes the serializer picks a slower format under memory pressure; that's been a rare edge.
[04:12] Samir: can you remind us of the test payload? we used the same tokenization and prompt seeds but i flagged the prompt length variability - some of our real traffic has longer tails.
[04:25] Oscar: yes, we kept the same distribution as you provided — mean 120 tokens, 95th 420 tokens. the throughput runs were capped at a 1k qps sustained for 20 minutes, bursts up to 2.5k.
[04:42] Evan: during that sustained window we saw good stability but when the burst hit the mixed nodes, the autoscaler lagged and some requests got queued, raising observed latency.
[04:58] Maya: right, that is an infra difference. two paths here: we can either request a short dedicated slot (reserved capacity) to eliminate autoscaler lag for the proof, or show how to tweak autoscaler and request sizing to match incumbent behavior.
[05:17] Anna: cost is a big consideration — incumbent offered a simpler fixed price for steady capacity. we need to demonstrate unit cost parity or improvement.
[05:30] Oscar: we prepared a unit cost per 1k tokens tab; median cost is down ~14% vs incumbent, but if you add the p99 tail impact and extra retries, that erodes savings.
[05:47] Priya: can you show the formula you used for retries?
[05:52] Oscar: it's in the spreadsheet — retries are counted when latency > 2s; we assumed exponential backoff and 1 retry on the client. but we can also run with zero-retry model to present raw service latencies.
[06:12] Evan: i will say, from a product perspective, p99 matters for our diagnostic UX. a single slow result is worse for clinicians waiting on a result.
[06:25] Maya: understood. so top priorities are: remove fallback-run outliers for steady-state comparison, replicate the cold-start scenario with instrumented tracing, and try a short dedicated slot to show steady p99 under load.
[06:42] Samir: how quick can you spin a dedicated slot?
[06:46] Lina: for the POC we can provision a temporary dedicated slot in 24 hours if accepted. there are a couple steps for network and key provisioning though.
[06:58] Priya: for that we'll need the KMS integration checklist and SAML SSO guidance. security has to sign off.
[07:06] Maya: yes, i'll drop the security pack and the KMS steps in the follow-up.
[07:12] Anna: also include SOC2 scope and audit log retention; our compliance team will look at that first.
[07:19] Oscar: noted. we also saw a particular pattern: the p95 jumps correlate with large KV cache misses that cascade into higher kernel CPU on the serving host. adding a tiny async deserialization thread pool improved tail in our lab by ~60ms.
[07:40] Evan: could that introduce more complexity on your side? we are wary of more moving parts.
[07:46] Oscar: minimal — the change is local to runtime; no infra changes. we can ship a build for you to test in staging.
[07:58] Priya: if it's a runtime patch, how do we validate safety? can we run it in canary behind a flag?
[08:05] Lina: yes, canary is easy — the console supports weighted rollouts and rollback. we'll include instructions.
[08:15] Maya: ok next, questions from Triton: anything on data residency / logs?
[08:20] Samir: particularly the audit log write path; the incumbent pushes logs to our on-prem SIEM — can Redwood forward to a customer-managed endpoint?
[08:30] Oscar: yes, we support forwarders to customer endpoints and we can do syslog, S3, or direct webhook depending on your SIEM. we'll include an example config.
[08:41] Evan: perfect.
[08:44] Speaker 2: [laughs]
[08:50] Maya: quick recap before deeper bench talk: action items, dates — we'll put them in the deck.
[09:00] Oscar: back to bench detail: i want to call attention to the behavior under the 95th influx test. we saw a small throttling interaction in the autoscaler which queued requests and created a compounding effect - reminiscent of a convoys effect.
[09:18] Priya: is that kube scaler or cloud provider autoscaling?
[09:22] Oscar: cloud provider autoscale with cluster-autoscaler on top; we saw pod scale-up not fully amortizing for the 30s window. increasing min nodes or changing the scale window reduced the effect in our sim.
[09:36] Samir: we can try min nodes+1 for the next run.
[09:40] Maya: great. one more piece — we want to quantify the cold-cache penalty; Oscar will attach a cold-vs-warm csv where cold means idle > 10 minutes.
[09:52] Evan: thanks, that will help.
[09:55] Lina: i also want to flag that some transcription in the logs' service names got munged — e.g., 'kv-cach' shows up as 'k v dash c a s h' in a few places; it's a parsing artifact in our exporter. ignore that in the CSV key.
[10:08] Priya: noted.
[10:10] Anna: ok are we aligned on next run configs? so: no fallbacks, min nodes +1, instrument KV traces, and one dedicated-slot run?
[10:21] Maya: yes, and we'll deliver the annotated results and a cost delta comparison.
[10:26] Evan: last quick ask — could you also run a single-shot sensitivity test with our longest prompt (1.2k tokens) to see p99 behavior?
[10:35] Oscar: yes, we'll add that to the bench matrix.
[10:40] Speaker 3: (inaudible)
[10:50] Maya: perfect. i'll follow up after the call with links: perf CSV, security checklist, dedicated slot requisition form, and proposed next-run windows.
[11:02] Anna: thanks all.
[11:05] End meeting.

Notes/links referenced: perf-sheet.csv (link shared in chat), security-pack.pdf (link), dedicated-slot-request.form (link).

Transcript quality notes: automated transcription with periodic speaker merge issues; timestamps approximate. Some proper nouns (model variant names, service names) may be mis-capitalized or misspelled.
